# Tech Giants Cut Jobs to Fund AI, While Money Circulates Among Giants—What's Going On?

I recently saw a Reddit post and comments that deeply analyzed today's "AI hype" and criticized how capital is playing the AI narrative:\
https://www.reddit.com/r/ArtificialInteligence/comments/1oj52xx/tech\_companies\_are\_firing\_everyone\_to\_fund\_ai\_but/

China's capital market has also been hyping AI (especially hardware) for quite a while—some narratives even reach "the U.S. is running out of electricity" levels. Based on that article, I want to talk about the phenomenon: big tech companies are laying people off while pouring massive money into AI. What is behind this, and how should ordinary people view it rationally?

## 1. The Core Tension: Why Layoffs and AI Spending Coexist

First, the headline contradiction: layoffs have continued across tech. For example, [Amazon reportedly planned to cut 30,000 jobs](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/10/27/amazon-to-announce-sweeping-corporate-job-cuts-starting-tuesday.html), the largest in its history. Microsoft cut 15,000, Meta cut 3,600, Google cut hundreds. So far, 2025 tech layoffs have exceeded 180,000.

In sharp contrast, these companies keep increasing AI investment. In 2025, total AI spending across big tech exceeded $300 billion, far more than the costs saved via layoffs. Many companies also justify layoffs with "AI replacement" narratives:

* Zuckerberg: AI can do the work of mid-level engineers in writing code
* Amazon CEO: many roles will not require humans in the future
* Salesforce: cut 4,000 support staff due to expanded AI usage
* IBM: cut 8,000 HR roles claiming AI can handle administrative work

That leads to a key question: if AI replaces jobs and reduces costs, why does spending massively exceed savings? Where is the money going?

## 2. Where the Money Goes: A Closed Loop Among Giants?

The Reddit post argues that AI money largely circulates among tech giants, creating the appearance of growth without necessarily generating new profits.

::: center



Examples of the cross-loop:

* Microsoft buys Nvidia chips and also rents AWS services
* Amazon buys Nvidia chips and also uses Microsoft software
* Meta buys Nvidia chips and rents infra from Google Cloud and AWS
* Even Apple largely rents Google/AWS/Azure instead of building full AI infra itself

Money forms loops: Apple pays Google for services; Google buys Nvidia chips; Nvidia pays TSMC; Microsoft pays Amazon for cloud; Amazon pays Microsoft for software. From a financial reporting perspective, everyone looks like they are growing—but profits are not necessarily new.

The "Magnificent 7" (Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Tesla) together have about $17T market cap (U.S. GDP ~ $30T). But in 2024 their combined revenue was ~$2.2T and net profit ~$550B. Their average P/E is ~35, while the rest of S\&P 500 averages ~15.5.

Investors accept high valuations because they expect AI to generate profits later. Yet in current reality, aside from Meta having some AI-related revenue, most AI spending has not become clear profit.

Worse, there is a spending inertia: if a company reduces AI investment, the stock may drop immediately because the market reads it as "giving up AI". So even without profits, companies keep spending, creating an AI arms race.

Capex growth reinforces this: in 2024, Microsoft/Amazon/Alphabet/Meta capex grew 42% YoY; in 2025 they planned another 17% increase. Just these four could spend ~$244B capex in 2025, much of which flows to Nvidia → TSMC → ASML, again forming loops.

This also links to ordinary people: much of U.S. retirement savings (401k) sits in S\&P 500 index funds, meaning a meaningful portion is indirectly betting on the Magnificent 7 AI story.

## 3. A Mix of Views from Reddit Comments

The comment section included many positions. A few representative themes:

1. **Where do laid-off workers go?** Some argued that AI now becomes a survival tool: employers use AI to screen resumes, job seekers use AI to write resumes.

2. **This is not a bubble, it's infrastructure.** Others argued compute is the competitive moat, and infrastructure build-out takes 10–15 years.

3. **ROI transparency is missing.** Companies spend billions yet rarely explain what value AI spending yields; measurement frameworks should become standard.

4. **What should ordinary people do?** Do not panic, but abandon the illusion of stable big-tech jobs; learn AI tools and stay competitive. "You do not control the market cycle; you control whether you are the one being cycled."

5. **Small companies get squeezed.** Big players can cut prices and crowd out startups that cannot get chips or cloud discounts.

6. **AI replaces some roles, not all.** Repetitive roles can be automated; high-end work still needs humans.

7. **Supply chain risk.** Too much dependence on Nvidia + TSMC creates systemic fragility.

8. **Consumer impact.** Cloud prices and subscription costs may rise under the banner of "AI upgrades".

9. **Regulation.** Some called for clearer disclosure on AI spending and its labor-market impact, plus antitrust.

## 4. Closing: How Should We View This AI Wave?

AI clearly has real value: it can raise efficiency and improve services. But there is also plenty of "false heat": layoffs justified by AI narratives, growth optics created by closed-loop spending, and risks pushed onto investors, ordinary people, and smaller companies.

Different groups should react differently:

* Tech workers: learn AI tools and move toward higher-end work that is harder to replace; avoid tying your career to a single company.
* Investors: focus on real AI revenue and business models, not only narratives.
* Consumers: be cautious about price increases justified as "AI upgrades"; watch where savings are invested.
* Policymakers: require disclosure, strengthen antitrust, support smaller companies, and reduce single-point supply chain risk.

In the end, the AI narrative must land in people's phones and computers—not remain only inside data centers.

# Memories Worth Revisiting
> Author: [Zhu Anfeng](https://zhuanfeng.netlify.app/)
>
> Website: <https://zhuanfeng.netlify.app/>

### **Jingde Football Memories Series**

The *Football Memories of Jingde* series, originally published on QQ Zone around 2008, records the many small moments in which football accompanied me from childhood into adulthood, and shows how deeply the game shaped my life and relationships.

* In [Football Memories of Jingde (I)](/en/article/football-memories-jingde-first-article/), I look back on how my earliest interest in football was influenced by my mother. In third grade, after I kicked a basketball out of shape, I was scolded by her and did not touch football again until I moved into town for school.

* [Football Memories of Jingde (II)](/en/article/football-memories-jingde-second-article/) tells the story of my school years after moving into town. Although I became fascinated with arcade games, football memories still ran deep. In junior high, the school lacked proper sports facilities, so we kicked mineral-water bottles around as makeshift footballs. In high school, my classmates and I enjoyed the game as much as we could with very limited resources.

* By [Football Memories of Jingde (III)](/en/article/football-memories-jingde-third-article/), I was in my senior year of high school and had become deeply interested in both football and *Winning Eleven*. I remember the time spent gaming and playing football with classmates, as well as the competition and friendship between classes, especially our match against Class 1 and two especially gifted players, He Jinwei and Wang Zhengqiang.

* In [Football Memories of Jingde (IV)](/en/article/football-memories-jingde-forth-article/), I describe Wang Zhengqiang's skill and personality. He was not much of a drinker, but he was superb on the pitch and a key figure in our football circle. I also write about the regret of never really getting the chance to play alongside him more deeply.

* Finally, [Football Memories of Jingde (V)](/en/article/football-memories-jingde-fifth-article/) is a heartfelt remembrance of Zhang Qipei, my friend of seventeen years. Football brought us together, and we shared many unforgettable years. I write there about his nickname, "Tractor," his unique style on the pitch, and the literary talent and sensitivity that left a lasting impression on me. He passed away on November 17, 2021, and that piece is written in his memory.

The whole series is not only about football, but also about youth, friendship, and growing up. Through football, I built deep bonds with my friends, and those memories became an indispensable part of our lives.

### **Scattered Sparks of Memory**

These pieces record many scenes and reflections from student life through adulthood, revealing personal growth, friendship, a love of football, and a deeper way of thinking about life.

[Memories of the 5460 China Alumni Directory](/en/article/memories-5460-china-alumni-directory/): I revisit a message I left on the 5460 alumni site in 2000, one of the oldest traces of myself I can still find on the internet. It makes me reflect on how the online world has changed and how time has flowed by.

[Football Memories of Anzi](/en/article/football-memories-of-zhuanfeng/): Li Yu recalls the friendship we shared in college and our football experiences together. The piece captures my personality, playing style, and the joy of university life shaped by football.

[The 2003 Peking University Graduation Farewell Match](/en/article/football-farewell-match-graduation-2003/): Li Yu offers a detailed recollection of the CS99 team's farewell match in 2003, full of vivid moments from the game and the emotions among teammates. It stands as a symbol of youth and friendship as much as of football itself.

[May Day Odds and Ends](/en/article/he-trivialities-of-may-day/): A record of the small moments of my May Day holiday in 2008, including gatherings with friends, expectations for the future, and scattered details of ordinary life.

[The Sea, Endless Drifting](/en/article/essay-business-trip-sea/): Written on May 19, 2008, this piece reflects on a drifting life through the metaphor of travel, exploring uncertainty and the instability of the future.

[Early Spring, 2009](/en/article/early-spring-2009/): A short reflection from March 9, 2009 on a new year, the future, and a quietly positive attitude toward life and growth.

[Standing at the North Pole](/en/article/standing-at-the-north-pole/): Written on June 26, 2009, this piece uses the metaphor of standing at the North Pole to express confusion about direction in work and life, while still holding on.

[My 2011](/en/article/my-2011/): A reflection on the passing of time, on 2011, and on hopes for what comes next.

[In the Tall Birch Forest, My Youth Wanders](/en/article/in-the-tall-birch-forest-my-youth-wanders/): A poetic remembrance of youth and wandering, full of nostalgia for the past and longing for the future.

# Tech Notes
> Author: [Zhu Anfeng](https://zhuanfeng.netlify.app/)
>
